title: Heard and remembered
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: the sages ask Manu for the dharma, and Bhrigu tells it: why a law book calls itself remembered
carry: shruti is heard; smriti is remembered, and gives way
tomorrow: can an old rule be right for its age and wrong for ours?

lines: WHY CALL A LAW BOOK REMEMBERED?
cards: The Manusmriti opens like a story. The great sages come to Manu as he sits, his mind collected, and ask him: tell us the dharma of every people, in order. Manu begins.
Then he does something odd. He says the Creator taught this to him, he taught it to the sages, and now one of them, Bhrigu, will tell it all to you. And Bhrigu takes over.
So the book arrives passed hand to hand, told by someone who remembers. The name it's known by says so: Manusmriti, Manu's smriti, and smriti means what is remembered.
Why would a law book call itself remembered, and not heard?

teach.b: The book answers in its second chapter. Shruti, what is heard, is the Veda.
Smriti, what is remembered, is the books of dharma. The Veda is received, heard by the seers; the law books are remembered and handed on by people, the way Bhrigu hands on Manu.
That's a ranking, and the tradition built a rule on it. The Mimamsa Sutra, an old manual for reading the Veda, takes up the case where a smriti and the Veda disagree.

teach.h: WHERE THEY CLASH, SMRITI GIVES WAY.
teach.b: Its answer, in paraphrase: where they conflict, the smriti is set aside. So the puzzle solves itself. A law book calls itself remembered because it sits one step below what is heard.
And that step gives readers a door: a line in a law book can be put down without leaving the tradition. Some later readers use that door.
They ask of a verse: does this rest on the Veda, or on the custom of one time and place? And yesterday's boy came from the other shelf. The Chandogya is an Upanishad, counted among what is heard.
So when someone in the family says 'it's in the scriptures', a Hindu can fairly ask: which shelf, heard or remembered?

how: Hindu teachers distinguish shruti, the Veda, from smriti, the remembered books such as the dharma books, and some study groups ask which lines rest on the Veda and which on the custom of a time and place.

games.q: what does “with the keeper's framing of what” mean?
o: what a tradition holds on to and lets go
the debts a family owes its ancestors
the parts of a rite a priest may skip

games.q: heard and remembered — tap the pairs.
p: what is remembered: the dharma books
where they clash, smriti gives way
tells the book Manu taught him

s: smriti means made-up stories nobody believes
it means what is remembered: the dharma books, handed on by people.
the Manusmriti itself says smriti means the books of dharma
its second chapter: shruti is the Veda, smriti the dharma books.

games.q: a dharma book and an Upanishad seem to say different things on the same question. by the old Mimamsa rule, which governs where they truly clash?
o: the Upanishad: it's shruti, and the smriti gives way.
the dharma book, since it gives more detail.
whichever one your family happens to own.
games.why: the remembered gives way to the heard: where a smriti conflicts with the Veda, the Mimamsa Sutra sets the smriti aside. the Upanishads are counted as shruti.

practice: If there's paper near you, write one thing you were told is 'in the scriptures'. Beside it, write which shelf you think it sits on: heard, the Veda and Upanishads, or remembered, the dharma books and custom.
If you don't know, write a question mark; that's honest too. Look at the line, and breathe with it, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Kept and rejected, through one old pair of words: shruti, what is heard, and smriti, what is remembered, and so can be weighed.

orig.note: Sanskrit smriti, what is remembered: the name for the dharma books, one step below the Veda.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: shruti is heard; smriti is remembered, and where they clash, the remembered gives way. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manusmriti 1.1–4 and 1.58–60 (the great sages approach Manu and ask for the dharma; Manu says he learned it from the Creator and taught the sages, and Bhrigu will recite it in full)
Manusmriti 2.10 (shruti is the Veda, smriti the dharma books)
Mimamsa Sutra 1.3.3 (where smriti conflicts with the Veda, it is disregarded)
